peruse

puh-ROOZ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To peruse is to read something carefully and thoroughly.

At the diner, the regular customer always perused the same menu for a full five minutes before ordering the exact same thing she always does.

Example

Before the manuscript went to the printer, the editor perused every page one final time, catching two typos the earlier proofreaders had missed.

Peruse describes reading a text closely and attentively, not glancing at it or flipping through it quickly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

study: To study something is to read or examine it in order to learn it — you study a textbook before an exam, absorbing and memorizing with a goal in mind. To peruse is about the careful reading itself: attentive and thorough, but with no test to pass at the end.

examine: To examine is to look something over closely — a doctor examines a patient, a mechanic examines an engine, and neither is reading. To peruse is narrower: it applies only to text, read carefully line by line, and it carries no hint of suspicion or inspection.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

skim: to glance over something quickly without careful reading

glance: to look at something very briefly

Where it sits · how thoroughly it is examined

check → peruse → dissect

check vs. peruse: To check something is to give it a quick look to confirm a single detail, far less thorough than perusing it.

dissect vs. peruse: To dissect something is to break it down and analyze every part in extreme detail, going further than simply perusing it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together: Peruse's exact origin is debated among word historians -- it may combine the Latin prefix per- ('thoroughly') with an old form of the verb use, though no one is fully certain. What's clear is the meaning: to read or examine something thoroughly and carefully, not just glance at it.

Why its origin is uncertain: Word historians still debate where peruse came from; the best guess joins Latin per-, 'thoroughly,' to an old form of the verb use, but no one can prove it. What is certain is the sense that per- points to: thorough, careful reading -- not a quick skim.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Peruse is specifically about reading text (a book, a menu, a document) carefully. Compare it with scrutinize, which can apply to anything -- objects, data, people's behavior -- and usually implies a more suspicious, searching kind of inspection.
